blocks.text: An image is a two-dimensional function f(x, y) where x and y are the spatial coordinates and the value f(x, y) at any point is the intensity (brightness) at that location. In simpler terms: an image is a grid of measurements. Each measurement tells you how bright — or what colour — a particular point in the scene is.

For monochrome (black-and-white) images, the value f(x, y) represents brightness, often called the gray level. A colour image is not a single function but a combination of three separate 2D functions — one each for red, green, and blue in the RGB model. Every technique developed for monochrome images can generally be applied to colour images by processing each colour channel individually.

blocks.title: Continuous vs Digital
blocks.text: A photograph of the real world is continuous — coordinates and intensity can take any value. To process it on a computer, both must be made discrete through sampling and quantization.

lessons.title: How a Digital Image is Formed

blocks.text: A digital image does not exist naturally — it must be created by capturing and converting energy from the real world. The process has three stages.

steps.title: Energy and sensing
steps.text: A source of energy (commonly sunlight, but also X-rays, infrared, or radar) illuminates or passes through a scene. A sensor array — a grid of tiny light-sensitive elements — detects the reflected energy and converts it into continuous electrical voltage signals.

steps.title: Sampling (space discretisation)
steps.text: The continuous voltage signal from the sensor covers a continuous spatial area. Sampling divides that area into a finite grid of locations. Each location becomes one pixel. The density of this grid is the spatial resolution of the image.

steps.title: Quantization (intensity discretisation)
steps.text: At each sampled location, the continuous voltage must be rounded to one of a finite set of allowed values. The number of allowed values is determined by the bit depth: 1-bit gives 2 levels, 8-bit gives 256 levels, 24-bit gives 16.7 million colours.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine covering a painting with a net. Each cell of the net captures one colour value. A finer net (more cells) gives a more accurate reproduction; a coarser net loses detail.

blocks.question: An 8-bit grayscale image can store how many distinct intensity levels?
blocks.explanation: 8-bit means 2^8 = 256 possible values, ranging from 0 (black) to 255 (white).

blocks.text: Digital image processing is the manipulation of digital images using a computer. Because an image is a matrix of numbers, any mathematical operation that can be applied to a matrix can, in principle, be applied to an image.

blocks.title: Two output types
blocks.text: Processing pipelines produce either (1) images as output — the processed result is another image, e.g. a denoised photograph — or (2) attributes as output — extracted information, e.g. the number of cells in a microscope slide.

blocks.title: Enhancement vs Restoration
blocks.text: Enhancement is subjective — it makes an image look better to a human viewer. Restoration is objective — it attempts to reverse a known degradation process using a mathematical model.

blocks.question: Which processing step is OBJECTIVE, guided by a mathematical model?
blocks.explanation: Restoration is objective — it uses a known degradation model to mathematically reverse damage. Enhancement is subjective, aimed at human preference.

blocks.text: A complete system for digital image processing requires several hardware and software components working together: image sensors (input devices), specialised image processing hardware, a general-purpose computer, mass storage, image display, hardcopy devices, and networking.

blocks.title: Storage levels
blocks.text: A single uncompressed 1024×1024 grayscale image requires 1 MB. Storage is organised at three levels: RAM (short-term, fast), SSD/HDD (online, working datasets), and tape/optical (archival, long-term).
